cases.answer: Originally set for September 3 at 2:17 p.m. ET, the Sept. 3 attempt was scrubbed. NASA then planned mid‑September cryo checks and targeted late‑September launch opportunities (requested Sept. 23 and Sept. 27 and discussed a Sept. 17 cryo demo), with Sept. 27 (backup Oct. 2) as an early target if the demo succeeded. A Hurricane Ian rollback from the pad on Sept. 26 disrupted late‑September plans, and Artemis I ultimately launched successfully on November 16 at 1:47 a.m.

propositions.text: On Sept 2, NASA said the two‑hour launch window opened Sept 3 at 2:17 p.m. Eastern Time.
NASA waved off (scrubbed) the Sept 3 launch attempt due to a liquid hydrogen leak.
NASA stated it would not launch in launch period 25, which ended Sept 6.
After the scrub, NASA requested possible launch dates of Sept 23 and Sept 27 and targeted a Sept 17 cryo demonstration.
Assuming the cryo demo met objectives, NASA planned a launch attempt as early as Sept 27 with Oct 2 as a backup.
On the night of Sept 26, Kennedy began rolling Artemis I back to the VAB because of Hurricane Ian.
Artemis I successfully launched on Nov 16 at 1:47 a.m..

cases.answer: NASA said the September 3 scrub was caused by a large liquid hydrogen leak in the core-stage fill system — a leak at the 8‑inch quick‑disconnect on the tail service mast umbilical that began when the flow transitioned from slow fill to fast fill; teams also noted an earlier inadvertent overpressurization of the hydrogen transfer line (to ~60 psi vs the planned ~20 psi) that may have affected the seal and planned to replace the quick‑disconnect soft‑goods/seal.

propositions.text: NASA said the launch attempt was waved off because teams encountered a liquid hydrogen leak while filling propellant into the core stage.
NASA identified a large leak at the 8‑inch quick‑disconnect on the tail service mast umbilical.
NASA said the leak started when operations transitioned from slow fill to fast fill.

NASA reported an earlier inadvertent pressurization of the hydrogen transfer line up to about 60 psi (versus the planned ~20 psi) and said it might have affected the seal but that it was too early to be certain.
NASA said teams planned to remove and replace the quick‑disconnect soft goods/seal to address the leak.

cases.answer: NASA said teams removed and replaced the soft‑goods seals on the 8‑inch fill/drain quick‑disconnect (and the 4‑inch bleed QD) at the TSMU by demating the ground and flight plates, installing transport caps and a protective enclosure (a plastic tent with conditioned air) to do the R&R on the pad, then remaking the plates and doing retests. They described a planned cryogenic demonstration (targeted around Sept. 17) as an objective‑based test to verify the new seals under cryogenic conditions by tanking the core stage and the ICPS with LH2 and LO2, doing an engine bleed/chilldown and a pre‑press demonstration to check valve timing and to monitor the LH2 tank; the team called the new approach a “kinder, gentler” loading (slower, steady pressure ramps, controlled valve movement and thermal conditioning to reduce pressure/thermal shocks) and said the demo would stop short of terminal count.

propositions.text: NASA removed and replaced the soft‑goods seals on the 8‑inch fill/drain quick‑disconnect and the 4‑inch bleed quick‑disconnect at the TSMU.
To access the quick disconnects they demated the LH2 TSMU plate from the flight plate, installed transportation caps and a plate cover to protect against contamination.
Workers set up an enclosure (described like a plastic tent) with conditioned air around the flight plate to protect hardware and personnel while performing the R&R on the pad.
The plan was to complete the R&R, remake the plates, do a mini integrated verification/retreat test and then a cryogenic demonstration.
NASA set a target date (around September 17) for the cryogenic demonstration to verify the repaired seals under cryogenic conditions.
The cryogenic demonstration was described as an objective‑based test that would tank the core stage and the ICPS with liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
The demo would include an engine bleed/chilldown and a pre‑press demonstration to verify valve timing and would monitor the core LH2 tank.
NASA said the demonstration would not go into terminal count and emphasized a 'kinder, gentler' loading approach.

The 'kinder, gentler' approach involves slower, steady pressure ramps on the LH2 sphere, controlled main fuel valve operation, and thermal conditioning to reduce pressure and temperature shocks on the seals.
NASA characterized replacement of the soft goods as the leading suspect solution and said a pad cryo test is the only way to fully validate the seals at cryogenic temperatures.

cases.answer: The archive says Hurricane Ian was seen from space as it intensified and made landfall in southwest Florida as a Category 4 storm, and NASA began rolling Artemis I off Launch Pad 39B back into the Vehicle Assembly Building the night of Sept. 26. Managers said the rollback was driven by weather predictions related to Hurricane Ian and to give employees time to attend to family needs. NASA also noted that a decision to roll back for a hurricane is typically made about three days out and that, in the vehicle’s current state, a rollback would take about three days.

propositions.text: External cameras aboard the International Space Station captured Hurricane Ian south of Cuba on September 26.
Space station cameras captured Hurricane Ian again on September 28 as it made landfall in southwest Florida as a Category 4 storm with winds around 155 mph.
On the night of September 26, Kennedy Space Center began moving the Artemis I Space Launch System rocket and Orion spacecraft from Launch Pad 39B back into the Vehicle Assembly Building.
Managers decided the rollback because of weather predictions related to Hurricane Ian and to give employees time to address the needs of their families.
NASA said a decision to roll back for a hurricane is typically made about three days before impact.
NASA said that, in the vehicle’s then-current configuration, it would take about three days to roll back to the Vehicle Assembly Building.

cases.answer: The archive contains no statement identifying anyone as intentionally sabotaging the Artemis I launch schedule.
Yes. Multiple NASA officials repeatedly stated they would not launch until the vehicle was ready.

propositions.text: At the September 3 post‑scrub news conference, NASA leadership said "We do not launch until we think it's right." (m-z-019f9fa5-dca0-7d03-b2f4-094ed47f6570 167.79-172.75).
The same briefing reiterated "we're not going to launch until it's right" as standard operating procedure. (m-z-019f9fa5-dca0-7d03-b2f4-094ed47f6570 211.70-215.30).
Mike Sarafin echoed the same principle: "we're not going to launch till we're ready" / "we will fly when we're ready." (m-z-019f9fa5-dca0-7d03-b2f4-094ed47f6570 871.68-875.84).

In the September 19 pre‑demonstration briefing, NASA again stated the policy of launching only when ready. (m-z-019f9fbd-2c83-73b2-8935-2c71e6155ec4 677.83-684.15).

cases.answer: No. NASA said the hydrogen transfer line was inadvertently overpressurized during the Sept. 3 chilldown but told reporters it was too early to conclude that overpressurization caused the leak and that a fault‑tree analysis was required; later inspections showed a small indentation in the 8‑inch quick‑disconnect seal but NASA did not state a single conclusive root cause attributing the leak solely to the pressurization.

propositions.text: NASA reported an inadvertent overpressurization of the hydrogen transfer line during the Sept. 3 chilldown that rose to about 60 psi (exceeding their planned ~20 psi).
NASA stated it was too early to tell if that inadvertent overpressurization was the cause of the Sept. 3 hydrogen leak and said a fault‑tree analysis was required before concluding causation.
NASA noted a wrong valve command occurred briefly in the sequence and emphasized that correlation does not equal causation while they investigate.
Subsequent inspections of the 8‑inch quick‑disconnect revealed a small indentation (a witness mark) in the seal; no piece of foreign object debris was recovered.
NASA did not announce a single, conclusive root cause in the archive material and therefore did not conclusively determine that the inadvertent pressurization caused the Sept. 3 leak.

cases.answer: The September 3 launch attempt was scrubbed because teams detected a large liquid hydrogen leak in the LH2 fill/transfer umbilical during cryogenic loading — a leak at the 8‑inch quick disconnect that began when going from slow to fast fill after an inadvertent overpressurization of the hydrogen transfer line (to about 60 psi). Multiple troubleshooting attempts could not stop the leak, hydrogen concentrations exceeded flight safety limits, and the launch was waved off (scrub declared) and the vehicle safed and drained.

propositions.text: NASA waved off the September 3 Artemis I launch attempt after teams encountered a liquid hydrogen leak while filling propellant into the core stage.
During chill down a hydrogen transfer line was inadvertently overpressurized (to about 60 psi).
A large hydrogen leak occurred at the 8‑inch quick disconnect of the LH2 umbilical when transitioning from slow fill to fast fill.
Teams attempted multiple times (three tries) to resolve/reseat the leak but were unsuccessful.
Hydrogen concentrations during the leak exceeded the allowable safety limit (about four percent) by roughly two to three times.
The scrub was declared (11:17 Eastern Time), the vehicle was safed, and propellants were drained following the unresolved leak.

cases.answer: The archive contains no statement that any NASA official said alien interference delayed Artemis I; no evidence in the provided recordings supports that claim.

No. The archive shows multiple causes (notably a large liquid hydrogen leak and required seal repairs, plus range/FTS scheduling constraints) in addition to Hurricane Ian; Ian was not established as the sole cause of the November launch.

propositions.text: A liquid hydrogen leak during tanking on September 3 caused NASA to wave off the Artemis I launch attempt.
The leak during the September attempt was characterized as a large leak at the 8-inch quick disconnect requiring removal and replacement of soft goods/seals.
Teams considered repair options (replace seals at the pad or roll back to the VAB) and planned a cryogenic demonstration/test to verify the seals.
Project managers stated that the required repair options would not preserve the ability to fly before the end of the current launch period without additional actions.
Managers rolled the Artemis I vehicle back into the Vehicle Assembly Building ahead of Hurricane Ian on/about September 26 due to weather predictions.
Range/flight-termination-system retest requirements and range scheduling were additional constraints affecting whether the vehicle could remain on the pad and the launch schedule.

cases.answer: Range retest rules for the flight‑termination system (FTS) created a timing constraint: unless the Range approved an extension/waiver, NASA would have to roll SLS back to the VAB to retest or replace FTS batteries rather than keep the vehicle on the pad — so NASA submitted waiver requests (proposing Sept. 23 and Sept. 27 planning dates) to try to stay on pad; without Range approval they planned to roll back and retest (noting a rollback would be required after the retest interval).

propositions.text: The Eastern Range enforces retest requirements for the flight‑termination system that limit how long the FTS batteries can remain untested on the pad.
Without a Range waiver/extension, NASA would have to roll the vehicle back to the Vehicle Assembly Building to retest or replace FTS batteries.
NASA submitted a waiver request and proposed September 23 and September 27 as planning launch dates while negotiating an extension with the Range.

NASA planned that, if they could not meet the retest interval on pad (e.g., past the specified date), they would roll back and retest the FTS (noting a rollback after the interval such as after Sept. 6).
